source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, Tables 1 and 8 (re-read from PDF)
finding: Self-generated exemplars beat 0-shot CoT and 5-shot CoT on GPT-3.5, but the margin over 5-shot CoT is small, and plain self-consistency adds much more.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo GSM8K: 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated exemplars 77.8 (+1.1 over 5-shot). MATH: 33.0, 33.9, 34.9, 37.3 (+2.4). Table 8: adding self-consistency to the method gives GSM8K 85.3 (+7.5) and MATH 46.0 (+8.7). Codeforces GPT-4 Acc@1/Acc@10: 0-shot 16/30, best variant (knowledge + exemplars) 19/37.
limits: Table text is garbled in the PDF; row order inferred from the four values per column and from claim K13. No CIs, no seeds. No equal-token comparison: the method spends output tokens writing exemplars, and extra samples via self-consistency were worth more than the method itself. Table 4 shows the method loses to retrieved 5-shot on small models.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly answered: on the original models the gain over 5-shot is +1 to +2 points, smaller than the gain from voting. An equal-token test against N-sample voting was never run by the authors.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) scale ablation (Table 4 and section 6.4)
finding: Self-generated exemplars only work when the model is strong enough; with weak models retrieved exemplars win.
numbers: GSM8K with text-curie-001 and text-davinci-001: retrieved few-shot CoT better than the method. text-davinci-002 and -003: method better than fixed 5-shot CoT and retrieved 5-shot CoT.
quote: The downside of generation is that it may fail to produce valid exemplars if the LLMs are weak
limits: Only OpenAI completion-era models; a 2023 result.
agent_relevance: The method needs a model that already knows related problems. Newer, stronger models cross this threshold, so the open question is whether the gain vanishes because zero-shot is already strong (see d03).

source: Cheng et al. (2026, v3) Revisiting chain-of-thought prompting: zero-shot can be stronger than few-shot
finding: For recent strong models (Qwen2.5 series), adding CoT exemplars does not beat zero-shot CoT on GSM8K and MATH; even exemplars written by DeepSeek-R1 or Qwen2.5-Max do not help. Models seem to ignore the exemplars.
numbers: GSM8K and MATH, Qwen2.5-7B/14B/72B, settings: zero-shot, 8-shot, top-k retrieved, Fast-votek, R1-4shot, Qwen-8shot. Adding noise to exemplars (Noise50) did not lower accuracy in most settings; for 72B it matched or slightly beat the clean setting. Authors also report an evaluation bug in open-source harnesses that underestimated zero-shot GSM8K. I did not extract per-cell accuracies.
quote: models tend to ignore the exemplars and focus primarily on the instructions
limits: Open-weight Qwen models only, maths only. Exemplars here are labelled CoT demos, not analogues; the finding transfers to self-generated analogue exemplars only by inference.
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 2: suggests that exemplar-style analogue injection gives about zero gain on current strong models for maths, so any claim for an analogue step must be tested against a zero-shot baseline of the same model. Do not assume the 2023 gain survives.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1, prompt-engineering note
finding: The authors say R1 is sensitive to prompts and few-shot prompting consistently degrades it; they recommend zero-shot with a stated output format.
numbers: No numbers given for this statement.
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
limits: One sentence in the paper, no table. Reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: For reasoning-type models, example injection (including analogues) may hurt. Treat any analogue step as something that can lower accuracy and measure it.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction (Table 1)
finding: Asking the model to state the high-level principle first (explicit abstraction before solving) helps, and beats 1-shot exemplars. This is the closest tested relative of 'name the shared structure first'.
numbers: MMLU Physics / Chemistry. PaLM-2L: base 66.4/70.9, CoT 65.0/75.3, step-back 73.2/81.8. GPT-4: base 69.4/80.9, 1-shot 78.4/80.5, CoT 82.9/85.3, step-back 84.5/85.6. Llama2-70B: CoT 59.3/64.1, step-back 64.8/66.7.
limits: Not an analogy test. On GPT-4 the margin over CoT is +1.6 physics and +0.3 chemistry, within the reported SD (1.2 to 1.4). Models are 2023 vintage.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the abstraction step helps weaker models more (PaLM-2L +7 to +8 over CoT on physics and chemistry) than strong ones (GPT-4 +0.3 to +1.6). A 'name the shared structure' step probably has the same shape: big for weak models, small for strong ones. Untested for analogy per se.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Step-back error analysis, TimeQA
finding: Abstraction first fixes many baseline errors but also introduces some new ones; the main remaining bottleneck is the reasoning step.
numbers: TimeQA PaLM-2L: baseline 41.5, CoT 40.8, step-back 66.0, step-back + RAG 68.7. Step-back fixes up to about 40% of baseline errors and introduces up to about 12% new errors (11.9% on TimeQA).
quote: Step-Back fixes a large portion of errors (up to 40%) while introducing a small portion of new errors (max 12%)
limits: PaLM-2L, 2023. Error rates are shares of cases, single run.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: an abstraction or analogue step has a measurable harm rate of about 12%, the same order as Ding's 25% upper bound. A code check on the final answer is the cheap screen, because the harm shows only in the answer.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners (ablations)
finding: Retrieving past successes by task similarity worked best; retrieving by reasoning-step similarity was a little worse; random retrieval was clearly worse. Insights extracted from success/failure pairs needed real experience.
numbers: ALFWorld ablation of in-context example selection: task-similarity (ExpeL) 59.0%; the table also shows 40.0, 48.5 and 42.5 but its row labels are garbled in the PDF text, so I do not assign them. Text: random sampling 'significant drop', reason similarity 'slightly drops'. HotpotQA: an agent that extracts insights only from the initial few-shots had no advantage over ReAct.
limits: gpt-3.5/gpt-4 era agents, 4-fold validation, small environments. Retrieval key compared is task text vs the latest reasoning step, not surface vs abstract structure.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for a lesson store keyed on the task, task-level similarity beat step-level similarity and random. Nothing here tests an abstracted-mechanism key against surface text.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL insight extraction from success/failure pairs and transfer
finding: ExpeL extracts rules by comparing a failed and a successful attempt at the same task (a pair), then reuses the rules on a new task type.
numbers: Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER success rate: ReAct baseline 58, ExpeL Transfer without task demos 63, ExpeL Transfer 65 (+/-1.7); a further row reads 70 but its label is garbled. ALFWorld with Reflexion rounds R0 to R3: retrieve-only 40.3 to 54.4; with insights 54.5 to 60.4; top row 59.0 to 64.2.
limits: No ablation isolating pair comparison from single-case summaries; transfer was one source/target pair. Table layouts are partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the nearest LLM version of analogical encoding (compare a failure and a success, write the rule) gives several points on a near-domain transfer. It is not a controlled test against a single-case lesson, so gap 5 stays open.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (abstraction vs concrete examples)
finding: Storing abstracted workflows (example-specific values replaced by placeholders) beat retrieving concrete full examples, and the benefit grew as the train-test gap widened.
numbers: Mind2Web cross-task, gpt-4: MindAct element accuracy 41.6, step SR 36.2; AWM 50.6 and 45.1. Versus Synapse (retrieves concrete examples) AWM +5.0 element accuracy and +4.0 step SR. Cross-website step SR 30.1 to 33.7 (offline) or 33.9 (online); cross-domain 18.6 to 32.6 / 35.5. Rule-based vs LM induction on Mind2Web cross-task: step SR 43.4 vs 45.1. WebArena rule 35.6 vs LM 35.5 (no gap).
limits: Full-task success rates are low (0.7 to 4.8% on Mind2Web), so the step-level gains matter more than the end gains. Abstraction is a bundle (sub-routines plus placeholders), not isolated.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a real test that abstracted content beats concrete episodes, especially across domains. It supports abstracted lessons over raw trajectories, but the retrieval key itself was not varied.

source: Wang et al. (2024) AWM, offline vs online distribution gap
finding: Workflows induced from the test queries themselves (online) generalise better when training and test tasks differ; offline training workflows can be wrong or mismatched.
numbers: Cross-domain Mind2Web step SR: AWM offline 32.6, online 35.5; success rate 0.7 vs 1.7. Abstract claims +8.9 to +14.0 absolute points over baselines as the gap widens.
limits: Authors state induced workflows are not always correct and can degrade performance.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a distance-dependent effect exists in agent memory: the further the new task is from stored tasks, the more it pays to build lessons online. Supports estimating distance per run rather than fixing it.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet (Table 1)
finding: A curated, abstracted memory of reusable strategies and code helps a lot where one trick transfers (Game of 24, equation balancing), and little or negatively where it does not.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024: baseline 23.3, DC-Cu 50.0, retrieval-only (DR) 43.3; AIME 2025 6.7 to 36.7. GPT-4o Game of 24: 10 to 99 (DC-RS). GPT-4o MMLU-Pro Engineering: baseline 53.2, DC-Cu 44.0 (drop). GPT-4o GPQA-Diamond: baseline 57.1, DR 55.1, DC-RS 57.1.
limits: AIME sets are 30 questions each, so one question is 3.3 points; single run, no CIs. Questions arrive in sequence within one benchmark, so some gain is within-benchmark leakage, not cross-domain transfer.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 9: curated lessons beat raw retrieval on most math tasks, and retrieval or memory can hurt a strong model (negative cells). Memory entries need a check that screens harm.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet, full-history vs curated (Table 2) and small models (Table 3)
finding: Appending everything is worse than curating; weaker models gain little or lose.
numbers: AIME 2024 Sonnet: baseline 23.3, full history (FH) 26.7, DC-Cu 50.0. GPT-4o: baseline 20.0, FH 13.3, DC-RS 40.0. AIME 2025 GPT-4o: baseline 6.7, FH 3.3, DC-RS 20.0. GPT-4o-mini AIME 2024: DC-Cu and DC-RS below baseline.
limits: N=30 per cell; very noisy.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: abstraction and curation (a schema step) beat verbatim storage by a large margin on the same model, an LLM echo of the human schema effect, but there is no pair-comparison arm.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet, retrieval confusion
finding: The authors say retrieval can in some cases introduce confusion, especially if suboptimal examples are recalled.
numbers: GPT-4o GPQA-Diamond: 57.1 baseline vs 58.1 DC-RS and 55.1 DR; MMLU-Pro Engineering 53.2 to 51.2 (DC-RS) and 48.8 (DR).
limits: Authors' explanation from output inspection; not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a retrieved analogue can lower accuracy by 2 to 5 points on knowledge tasks; harm is real for strong models. Use a code or answer check before keeping a lesson.

source: Si, Hashimoto & Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap
finding: Ideas the model made looked better than human ideas before execution, but after 43 experts spent 100+ hours executing them the lead disappeared and often flipped.
numbers: 43 expert researchers executed randomly assigned ideas (human N=19, LLM N=24 in the figure). Scores after minus before, 1-10 scale: human ideas novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052; LLM ideas -1.049, -1.760, -1.879. Differences significant on all four metrics (FDR-adjusted p 0.025 to 0.001). Example effectiveness: LLM 6.00 before, 4.13 after; human 4.83 before, 4.78 after.
limits: NLP research ideas, not design; the idea generator was the Si 2024 pipeline, not analogy-specific. 43 projects.
agent_relevance: Gaps 10 (indirect) and 6: the one finished-outcome test found for LLM ideation. Rated novelty at the idea stage overstates real value by 1 to 2 points; ratings of an idea do not predict what happens when it is run. Supports scoring analogues by executed outcome, not by self-rated usefulness.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2025) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs, PNAS Nexus
finding: The failure of GPT-4 on counterfactual (permuted-alphabet) letter-string analogies comes from counting errors, not from missing analogy. With code execution GPT-4 reaches human level.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). GPT-4 + code execution vs humans: P=0.92 (no difference); GPT-4 alone vs humans P<2e-16; GPT-4 + zero-shot CoT still below humans (P=3e-8) and below code (P=4.4e-5). Interval identification accuracy for GPT-4 10.8%. Control with code tool disabled 22.5% vs GPT-4 21.7%. 38% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% for humans.
limits: Same authors as the original claim. Letter-string tasks only; GPT-4 (2024 build). Not a far-vs-near test. Code does the indexing, so it shows the analogy rule was in the model, not that the model maps unfamiliar structure.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 9: the counterfactual failure (K12) is mostly a tool problem and a code check closes it. For our agent, a code-run step is the right fix for brittle mapping.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (Table 3)
finding: Asking a model to judge and revise its own answer without outside feedback lowers accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4 GSM8K: standard 95.5, self-correct round 1 91.5, round 2 89.0. GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: standard 75.8, round 1 38.1, round 2 41.8. HotpotQA GPT-4: 49.0 then 49.0 then 43.0.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 of 2023; intrinsic self-correction only (no code or tool). Row labels in the PDF table are garbled; values read by column order.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: indirect evidence that a model's own usefulness rating of an analogue should not be trusted without an external signal. No study rates analogue usefulness directly; this is the nearest check on self-judgement.

source: SSRN preprint (2026) Does memory credit travel? Paired factorial audits of LLM-agent memory
finding: Outcome after retrieving a memory is not the memory's own contribution; most apparent help is passenger credit.
numbers: ALFWorld, Qwen3-32B and Mistral Small 3.1-24B, 576 episodes. Bank-only success already 166/192 (86.5%). Of 169 joint successes a retrieval ledger would credit to the candidate, only 10 are marginal helps (5.9% precision) and 159 are passenger credit. Seven joint failures hide marginal harm. Bank context changes a candidate's effect in 35/192 strata.
limits: Abstract only (via Crossref), preprint, not peer reviewed; open models; the controller comparison was non-informative (identical mean regret 0.0521).
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 9: scoring a lesson by whether the run succeeded after retrieving it overcounts help by about 17 times here (169 credited vs 10 real). Need matched with/without runs to credit or blame an analogue.

source: Comparing analogy-based methods: bio-inspiration and engineering-domain inspiration for domain selection and novelty (Biomimetics 2024)
finding: Biological (far) analogies raised design novelty over within-domain (near) ones, but biological and cross-domain (middle) analogies did not differ, so a middle distance did as well as the farthest.
numbers: 26 teams of novice product designers, one analogical source from each of three domains. Biological analogies were chosen most often. Bio vs within: significant novelty gain. Bio vs cross: no significant difference.
limits: Abstract only (via Crossref). Small N, novices. Selection frequency is confounded with the attractiveness of the source.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a further datum for a plateau instead of a far-is-better rule: middle distance matches far. Fits a sweet-spot account but does not locate it.

source: Li, Zhang, Cao & Chen (2026) Beyond input-output: design-by-analogy in the generative AI era (survey), discussion sections
finding: The survey states design-by-analogy lacks rigorous empirical evaluation of AI outputs, and summarises distance guidance from earlier work.
numbers: Says optimal distance depends on stage (far for early vision, near for refinement), goal (quantity favours near, quality far) and expertise (novices near, experts far), citing earlier human studies [21, 25, 146]. Gap statement: significant lack of rigorous empirical evaluation of AI-driven DbA outputs.
limits: Secondary source; the expertise claim rests on human studies, not LLM runs. I did not trace its primary citations.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 10: confirms no one has run a rigorous expert or finished-design LLM DbA test; supports estimating distance per task stage.

source: Lin (2026) Generative AI as a cognitive support tool in early-stage design ideation, PLOS One
finding: In a counterbalanced experiment, AI help gave better problem framing and mechanism ratings but human-only work got higher ratings for innovation and solution strategy.
numbers: 32 undergraduate design students, within-subjects, 3 expert raters, six analytic criteria, Holm-Bonferroni correction. AI higher on problem framing, mechanism, creator and evaluator perspective; human-only higher on innovation and solution strategy; no robust difference on five design attributes of refined concepts.
limits: Not an analogy study (text-and-image AI workflow). Students, not professionals; one brief; abstract and page text read, tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the best 2026 controlled design-ideation test found with expert raters shows no uniform gain from AI and a loss on innovation. Be sceptical that generated stimuli raise originality.
